title: Shapley Neuron Values for Continual Learning: Which Neurons Matter Most?
topic: General Machine Learning->Transfer, Multitask and Meta-learning
claim: Important units are identified and frozen per task, with overlapping units shared across tasks while the remaining units stay plastic for new tasks.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, double arrows labeled Freeze, color legend below
description: Three copies of the same small fully connected network are arranged left to right and titled Task t-1, Task t and Task t+1. Each has two gray input nodes, three hidden layers of four neurons, and an output layer in a rounded box. Neurons are filled by the task in which they rank in the top r% by Shapley value: green for t-1, orange for t, cyan for t+1. Neurons that stay unfilled are plastic. Hatched neurons are shared across several tasks. Thick double arrows labeled Freeze, with C_t and C_{t-1} ∪ C_t, link the panels. The output layer gains more nodes at each step. Class-IL and Task-IL tags mark the output groups. A legend at the bottom explains the colors and the thresholds φ > τ.
caption: An illustration of Shapley Neuron Values where for each task task $t-1$, task $t$, and task $t+1$, we identify and freeze the Neurons whose Shapley Values fall within the top $r%$. Neurons marked with specific colors indicate that the same Neuron appears within the top $r%$ for $t$ specific tasks. $\tau_i$ is each task's top $r%$ threshold.
abstract: Continual learning enables neural networks to learn tasks sequentially without forgetting previously acquired knowledge. However, neural networks suffer from catastrophic forgetting, where learning new tasks degrades performance on earlier ones. We address this problem with Shapley Neuron Valuation (SNV), a principled framework that quantifies Neuron importance in continual learning, grounded in cooperative game theory. SNV selectively freezes important Neurons while keeping others plastic, enabling buffer-free continual learning without expanding architecture. Experiments on ImageNet-1k show that SNV consistently outperforms existing buffer-free methods. In particular, SNV improves accuracy by +2.88% in the class incremental learning and +6.46% in the task incremental learning scenarios compared to the second baseline.
